facts.statement: British soldier, 1860–1933; enlisted 1877 and reached field marshal in 1920.
Chief of the Imperial General Staff during the First World War; differed with Lloyd George over strategy.
Memoir From Private to Field-Marshal published 1921.

en.tagline: From the ranks to the direction of Britain’s war.
en.intro: Robertson’s rise gave his memoir an exceptional shape. The young enlisted cavalryman became the professional head of the British Army during the First World War and eventually a field marshal.
en.orientation: The story is more than a sequence of promotions. It follows the acquisition of professional knowledge and the tensions between military advice and political authority.
origin: Born in Lincolnshire in 1860, he enlisted in 1877. His progress took him from the routines of a private soldier towards commissioned and staff service.
career: As Chief of the Imperial General Staff he argued for concentrating Britain’s principal effort against Germany on the Western Front. His disagreements with Lloyd George exposed the contested relationship between military judgement and government policy.
literature: From Private to Field-Marshal gives that career the form of a personal account. Its reflections on study, service and advancement should be read alongside the author’s defence of his wartime position.
en.legacy: Robertson’s historical distinction lies in the distance travelled through the army’s hierarchy and in the authority he exercised at its summit. The memoir retains the voice of a professional who believed hard-earned knowledge should govern decisions.
en.bridge: The book follows the making of that professional outlook from its earliest military beginnings.
